questions.q: What is exponential backoff, and why use it after a 429?
options: Retrying with a progressively longer delay (e.g. 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2s) instead of hammering the provider again immediately
Immediately retrying in a tight loop until the request succeeds
Switching permanently to a different programming language
Reducing your gas price on every retry
questions.explain: Retrying instantly in a loop just adds more load to an already-throttling provider; backoff spaces retries out, giving the limit time to reset.

questions.q: Why can't a browser wallet alone replace a dApp's backend?
options: It can sign and call the chain directly, but can't run on a schedule, index history, or hold a server-side API key
Wallets are only able to read ETH balances, nothing else
Wallets cannot connect to any blockchain network
Browser wallets are blocked from calling smart contract functions
questions.explain: A wallet is a user-side signing tool; it has no persistent server process, so it can't do always-on jobs like listening for events or managing sessions.

questions.q: Why does one stuck transaction (say, nonce 3) block every later transaction from the same account?
options: A node won't include a transaction at nonce N+1 until nonce N from that sender has already landed
Ethereum only allows one pending transaction per account at a time by protocol rule
Later transactions are automatically cancelled when an earlier one is slow
It doesn't — later nonces confirm independently of earlier ones
questions.explain: Nonces must be consumed in strict order, so nonce 4 and 5 can't be included until nonce 3 confirms, regardless of how valid they are on their own.

questions.q: In ethers.js v6, what two things does `new ethers.Contract(...)` need to let you call a read function?
options: The contract's address and its ABI
The contract's bytecode and its compiler version
The user's private key and a gas limit
The block number and a transaction hash
questions.explain: A Contract instance is built from the deployed address plus the ABI describing its functions; the provider supplies the connection.

questions.q: Where does an `emit`-ted Solidity event actually get stored?
options: In the transaction's logs — a separate, cheaper-to-write section of the receipt, not contract state and not a return value
In a dedicated events table inside the contract's own storage
It's sent directly to the caller's wallet as a push notification
It isn't stored anywhere — events exist only during execution
questions.explain: Events are written into the logs bloom/receipt data, which is cheaper to write than contract storage and is never returned to the caller like a function return value.

questions.q: What is a chain reorg?
options: The network replacing a set of previously-accepted blocks with a different set, after two competing chains briefly exist
A planned, scheduled upgrade to the Ethereum protocol
A user manually reversing their own transaction
A node provider changing which RPC method it supports
questions.explain: A reorg happens when a competing chain wins out over blocks a node had already accepted, discarding those blocks and everything only contained in them.

questions.q: What four jobs does a real, production-shaped event listener service do that a bare `contract.on(...)` call alone does not?
options: Connect through a resilient provider, catch up on missed events, listen live, and confirm before treating events as final
Compile the contract, deploy it, verify it, and audit it
Mint new tokens, burn tokens, pause the contract, and transfer ownership
Encrypt the RPC endpoint, rotate API keys, log in a user, and send an email
questions.explain: A raw .on() call only covers 'listen live' — a real service also needs a resilient connection, a backfill step for downtime, and a confirmation gate before acting on anything.

questions.q: What does a WebSocket subscription require that polling doesn't?
options: A `wss://` endpoint and a persistent connection the client must manage
A paid node provider plan — free tiers can never use WebSockets
A smart contract deployed specifically for event forwarding
Manual confirmation from the user for every event
questions.explain: Subscriptions need a WebSocket-capable endpoint (wss://) and keep a long-lived connection open, unlike the stateless request/response of polling over HTTPS.

questions.q: What three files define a subgraph, according to this lesson?
options: subgraph.yaml (manifest), schema.graphql (entities), and mapping.ts (event-to-entity logic)
index.js, package.json, and README.md
contract.sol, abi.json, and deploy.sh
manifest.json, query.graphql, and handlers.js
questions.explain: The lesson names these three specific files and previews that Lessons 13 and 14 cover the schema and mappings in depth.

questions.q: In the lesson's example GraphQL query, where do `first`, `orderBy`, `orderDirection`, and `where` come from?
options: They're generated automatically from the schema defined in Lesson 13 — no custom filtering or sorting code was written for them
They must be manually implemented in mapping.ts for every entity
They are special AssemblyScript functions called from within the schema file
They only work if the subgraph was published without curation signal
questions.explain: The lesson states this directly — these query arguments come free from the schema, which is the actual payoff of defining entities well back in Lesson 13.

questions.q: What three-step pattern does the lesson say every real fix for this problem follows?
options: Listen for the relevant events, write them into a queryable database, then query that database instead of the chain
Buy a faster RPC provider, increase the rate limit, and keep scanning logs the same way
Store the entire blockchain locally and run SQL directly against the raw block files
Ask users to submit their own transaction history manually
questions.explain: This listen → write → query pattern is the lesson's core takeaway and the job description of every indexer, managed or custom.

questions.q: What does the `@entity` directive do in a subgraph's schema.graphql?
options: Marks a GraphQL type as getting its own indexed, queryable table in The Graph
Marks a field as required (non-nullable)
Declares a GraphQL subscription endpoint
Imports a type definition from another subgraph
questions.explain: The lesson defines @entity as the addition to standard GraphQL SDL that tells The Graph a type should be its own indexed table.

questions.q: Why does this lesson's code call `feed.decimals()` instead of hardcoding 8 when scaling the price?
options: Not every feed uses the same number of decimals, and hardcoding it would silently break if the code is later pointed at a different feed
decimals() is required by Solidity syntax and cannot be omitted
Hardcoding 8 would cause the contract call to revert with an error
decimals() returns the feed's contract address, not a scaling factor
questions.explain: The lesson explains this explicitly — most USD feeds use 8 decimals but not all do, so calling decimals() avoids a silent, hard-to-catch bug.

questions.q: What specific gap did Chainlink Functions solve, per this lesson?
options: Running off-chain computation or an authenticated API call that a contract itself can't make, with results aggregated across a decentralized oracle network
Giving contracts the ability to directly modify another contract's storage
Eliminating the need for gas fees on any transaction
Replacing Ethereum's consensus mechanism with a faster alternative
questions.explain: Functions is described as solving the problem of needing real computation or authenticated API access a contract can't do itself, using the same independent-nodes-plus-aggregation pattern as price feeds.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about the feed's contract address used in the consumer contract's constructor?
options: It's hardcoded, because every supported asset pair on every supported network has its own fixed address published by Chainlink
It's generated dynamically at deploy time by the Chainlink CLI
It changes every time the price updates, so it must be fetched via an API call first
It's the same address across every network and every asset pair
questions.explain: The lesson explains that each asset pair, per network, has its own fixed, published feed address hardcoded into the constructor.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a single trusted server pushing data on-chain doesn't actually solve the oracle problem?
options: Because it's a single point of failure and trust — if that server lies or goes offline, every dependent contract inherits the failure directly
Because a single server technically cannot submit transactions to a blockchain at all
Because it works perfectly and fully solves the problem; the lesson presents no issue with it
Because smart contracts are physically incapable of reading data from any external account
questions.explain: The lesson calls this out directly: one server is functionally identical to trusting one company's API, which is the exact centralization smart contracts exist to avoid.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why isn't recovering the signing address from the signature enough on its own?
options: Because it's only one of three checks — the nonce and domain also have to be validated, or SIWE's safety guarantees don't actually hold
Because Ethereum signatures cannot be cryptographically recovered at all
Because the siwe library does not support signature recovery
It is enough; the lesson states no other checks are necessary
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that signature recovery is necessary but not sufficient — it's only one of three distinct checks a correct verification performs.

questions.q: In the flow this lesson describes, what happens before the wallet signs the SIWE message?
options: The backend generates and issues a nonce, which the frontend includes when building the message
The backend immediately starts a session with no prior steps
The user must manually type their private key into the frontend
The wallet generates its own message with no input from the frontend or backend
questions.explain: The six-step flow in the lesson starts with the backend issuing a nonce before the frontend builds and signs the message.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does "gasless" actually mean?
options: The user doesn't need to hold the native gas token to pay for the transaction themselves — someone else covers it; gas itself still has a real cost
The transaction consumes zero blockspace and has no cost to anyone
The contract executes without using any gas because it's marked view
The user pays gas in a different cryptocurrency chosen at random
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that gas doesn't disappear — gasless means the user isn't the one who has to hold and spend the token, not that the cost vanishes.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what two triggers does a Web3 session have to handle beyond a normal web session's logout?
options: A wallet disconnecting, and a wallet switching accounts
A browser tab closing, and a page refresh
A smart contract being upgraded, and a gas price spike
An RPC provider going offline, and a block reorg
questions.explain: The lesson lists these two Web3-specific triggers explicitly, each requiring the frontend to actively invalidate the session rather than just update local UI state.
